title: Part 2, Chapter 47
paragraphs: In which the account continues of how Sancho Panza behaved in his government

The history tells us that they led Sancho from the courtroom to a magnificent palace, where a table had been set with royal splendor in a vast hall. Trumpets blared as Sancho came into the room, and four pages stepped forward offering him water for his hands, which Sancho accepted with great dignity. The music stopped, and Sancho took his seat at the head of the table — the only seat there was, with only a single place laid. A figure who later turned out to be a physician stationed himself standing at Sancho's side, holding a whalebone wand in his hand. Then they lifted away a fine white cloth that had been covering fruit and a wide assortment of dishes of every kind; a man who appeared to be a student said grace, and one page tied a lace-trimmed bib around Sancho's neck while another, acting as head carver, set a plate of fruit in front of him. But he had barely tasted a bite when the man with the wand tapped the plate, and it was whisked away from him with astonishing speed. The carver promptly set another dish before him, and Sancho moved to try it; yet before he could even reach it, let alone taste it, the wand had already touched it and a page carried it off as quickly as the fruit had gone. Watching this, Sancho was bewildered, and glancing around from face to face, he asked whether this dinner was meant to be eaten like a conjurer's sleight-of-hand act.

The man with the wand answered, “It is not to be eaten, señor governor, except in the manner usual and customary on other islands where there are governors. I, señor, am a physician, and I draw a salary on this island to serve its governors in that capacity, and I care far more for their health than for my own. I study day and night, learning the governor's constitution thoroughly so that I can cure him if he falls ill. My principal duty is to be present at his dinners and suppers, permitting him to eat whatever I judge suitable for him and withholding whatever I believe will harm him or injure his stomach. That is why I ordered the plate of fruit taken away, as being too moist, and that other dish removed for being too hot and full of spices that provoke thirst; for the man who drinks too much destroys and burns up the radical moisture in which life itself resides.”
“Well then,” said Sancho, “that dish of roast partridges over there, which looks so appetizing, surely won't do me any harm.”
To this the physician replied, “Of those my lord the governor shall not eat a single one as long as I draw breath.”
“And why not?” said Sancho.

“Because,” the doctor answered, “our master Hippocrates, the polestar and guiding light of medicine, declares in one of his aphorisms _omnis saturatio mala, perdicis autem pessima_, which means ‘all overeating is bad, but overeating partridge is the worst of all.’”

“In that case,” said Sancho, “let the señor doctor look over the dishes on this table and pick out the one that will do me the most good and the least harm, and let me eat it without his tapping it with that stick of his; because by the life of the governor — and God grant I live to enjoy it — I am dying of hunger; and whatever the doctor may say, denying me food is the way to end my life, not to lengthen it.”

“Your worship speaks the truth, señor governor,” said the physician; “and so it is my judgment that your worship should not eat those stewed rabbits over there, since rabbit is a furry sort of food; that veal you might have sampled, if it had not been roasted and served with pickles, but as things stand it is out of the question.”

“That big dish steaming away farther down the table,” said Sancho, “looks to me like an olla podrida, and with the variety of things that go into such stews, I can hardly fail to hit on something tasty that agrees with me.”

“_Absit_,” said the doctor; “let no such base notion come near us! Nothing in the world provides poorer nourishment than an olla podrida. Save your ollas podridas for canons, or college rectors, or country weddings, but keep them off the tables of governors, where everything served should be delicate and refined. The reason is this: always, everywhere, and by everyone, simple medicines are valued above compound ones, because in the simple ones we cannot go wrong, while in the compound we can err merely by altering the proportions of their ingredients. What I believe the governor ought to eat now, to preserve and strengthen his health, is a hundred or so wafer cakes and a few thin slices of quince conserve, which will settle his stomach and aid his digestion.”
Hearing this, Sancho leaned back in his chair, looked the doctor over from head to foot, and in a grave voice asked him what his name was and where he had taken his studies.

He answered, “My name, señor governor, is Doctor Pedro Recio de Aguero. I come from a place called Tirteafuera, which lies between Caracuel and Almodóvar del Campo, on the right-hand side, and I hold my doctor's degree from the university of Osuna.”

At this Sancho, burning all over with fury, shot back, “Then let Doctor Pedro Recio de Malaguero, native of Tirteafuera — a place on the right-hand side as you travel from Caracuel to Almodóvar del Campo — graduate of Osuna, clear out of my sight this instant; or I swear by the sun I'll pick up a club and, starting with him, beat my way through every doctor on this island; at least every one I know to be ignorant, for learned, wise, sensible physicians I will honor and revere as if they were divine. I say it again: let Pedro Recio get out of here, or I'll take this chair I'm sitting on and smash it over his head. And if I'm called to answer for it, I'll acquit myself by saying I did God a service in killing a bad doctor — a public executioner. Now bring me something to eat, or else take back your government; a trade that won't feed the man who works it isn't worth two beans.”

The doctor was alarmed to see the governor in such a rage, and he would have made his own Tirteafuera straight out of the room had not a post-horn sounded in the street at that very moment; the carver, leaning his head out the window, turned back and announced, “It's a courier from my lord the duke — no doubt carrying some dispatch of importance.”

The courier entered, sweating and out of breath, and drawing a paper from inside his shirt, placed it in the governor's hands. Sancho passed it to the majordomo and told him to read the address, which ran as follows:
_To Don Sancho Panza, Governor of the Island of Barataria, to be delivered into his own hands or those of his secretary._

Hearing this, Sancho asked, “Which of you is my secretary?” “I am, señor,” said one of those in attendance, “for I can read and write, and I am a Biscayan.” “With that qualification thrown in,” said Sancho, “you could be secretary to the emperor himself; open this paper and see what it says.” The newly minted secretary did so, and after reading the contents declared it a matter to be dealt with in private. Sancho ordered the room cleared, keeping back only the majordomo and the carver; the doctor and the rest withdrew, and the secretary then read out the letter, which said:

It has reached my ears, Señor Don Sancho Panza, that certain enemies of mine and of the island intend to launch a furious assault on it some night — which night, I cannot say. You must stay alert and keep watch, so they do not catch you off guard. I also know through reliable spies that four men have slipped into the town in disguise to take your life, because they fear your great abilities; keep your eyes open, be wary of anyone who comes up to speak with you, and eat nothing that is set before you. I will see to it that help reaches you if you find yourself in trouble, but in everything you must act as your good judgment would lead one to expect. Written here, the sixteenth of August, at four in the morning.
Your friend, THE DUKE.

Sancho was astounded, and the bystanders pretended to be just as amazed; then, turning to the majordomo, he said, “The first thing we must do — and it must be done right now — is throw Doctor Recio into the lock-up; because if anybody means to kill me, it's him, and by the slowest and worst death there is, which is starvation.”

“And furthermore,” said the carver, “in my opinion your worship should eat nothing at all on this table, for the whole spread was a gift from some nuns; and as the saying goes, ‘behind the cross lurks the devil.’”

“I won't argue with that,” said Sancho; “so for now bring me a piece of bread and four pounds or so of grapes — no poison can hide in those; the plain truth is I cannot carry on without eating, and if we're to be ready for these battles hanging over us, we'd better be well provisioned, for it's the belly that keeps the heart going, not the heart the belly. And you, secretary, write back to my lord the duke and tell him that all his orders will be carried out to the letter, exactly as he commands; and convey to my lady the duchess that I kiss her hands, and beg her not to forget to send my letter and my bundle to my wife Teresa Panza by messenger — I'll count it a great kindness and will serve her in everything within my power; and while you're at it, you can slip in a kiss of the hand for my master Don Quixote, so he may see that I'm grateful bread; and being a good secretary and a good Biscayan, you may add whatever you please and whatever fits best. Now clear away this cloth and give me something to eat, and I'll be ready for every spy and assassin and enchanter that comes against me or my island.”
At that moment a page entered and announced, “There is a farmer here on business who wishes to speak with your lordship about a matter of great importance, so he says.”

“It's a strange thing,” said Sancho, “these men and their business; can they really be such fools as not to see that an hour like this is no hour for business calls? We who govern, we who sit as judges — aren't we men of flesh and blood? Aren't we entitled to the rest our bodies need, or would they have us carved out of marble? By God and on my conscience, if this government stays in my hands (and I have a feeling it won't), I'll bring more than one of these business callers to heel. Still, tell the good man to come in; but first make sure he isn't one of those spies, or one of my assassins.”
“No, my lord,” said the page, “he doesn't seem that sort, for he looks a simple soul, and either I know nothing at all or he's as good as good bread.”
“There is nothing to fear,” said the majordomo, “for all of us are here with you.”
“Carver,” said Sancho, “now that Doctor Pedro Recio is out of the room, would it be possible for me to eat something solid and substantial — even if it were only a piece of bread and an onion?”
“Tonight at supper,” said the carver, “everything the dinner lacked shall be made up, and your lordship will be left fully satisfied.”
“God willing,” said Sancho.
The farmer now came in — a fine-looking man whom you could tell from a thousand leagues away was an honest fellow and a good soul. The first thing he asked was, “Which one here is the lord governor?”
“Who else would it be,” said the secretary, “but the man seated in the chair?”

“Then I humble myself before him,” said the farmer; and dropping to his knees, he begged for the governor's hand to kiss. Sancho refused it and told him to get up and state his business. The farmer obeyed, and then said, “I am a farmer, señor, born in Miguelturra, a village two leagues from Ciudad Real.”
“Another Tirteafuera!” said Sancho; “go on, brother; I know Miguelturra well enough, I can tell you, for it isn't far from my own town.”

“The matter is this, señor,” the farmer continued: “by God's mercy I am married, with the leave and license of the holy Roman Catholic Church; I have two sons, both students — the younger studying for his bachelor's degree, the elder for his licentiate. I am a widower, for my wife died, or to put it more accurately, a bad doctor killed her on my hands by giving her a purge while she was with child; and if it had pleased God for the child to be born, and a boy, I would have set him to study to be a doctor, so he wouldn't have to envy his brothers the bachelor and the licentiate.”
“So if your wife hadn't died — or hadn't been killed — you wouldn't be a widower now,” said Sancho.
“No, señor, of course not,” said the farmer.
“Well, that much we've established,” said Sancho; “press on, brother, for this is an hour better suited to bed than to business.”

“Well then,” the farmer went on, “this son of mine who is to be the bachelor fell in love, in that same town, with a young lady named Clara Perlerina, daughter of Andres Perlerino, a very wealthy farmer; and this name Perlerines doesn't come to them through lineage or descent, but because the whole family suffers from palsy, and to dress it up they're called the Perlerines; though truth to tell, the young lady is fair as an Oriental pearl, like a flower of the field — when seen from the right side, that is; from the left, not so much, since on that side she's missing an eye she lost to smallpox; and although her face is thickly and deeply pockmarked, those who love her insist they're not pockmarks at all, but graves where the hearts of her suitors lie buried. She is so clean that, to keep from dirtying her face, she carries her nose tipped up, as the saying goes, so you'd swear it was running away from her mouth; and even so she looks remarkably well, because she has a wide mouth; and if she weren't short ten or a dozen teeth and grinders, she could stand comparison and competition with the loveliest of them. Of her lips I'll say nothing, for they're so fine and thin that if lips could be wound like thread, you could make a skein of them; but being a different color from ordinary lips, they're a marvel to behold — mottled blue, green, and purple. Let my lord the governor forgive me for painting in such detail the charms of one who sooner or later will be my daughter; for I love her, and to my eye there's nothing wrong with her.”
“Paint away as you please,” said Sancho; “the painting suits me, and if I had dined, no dessert could please my palate better than your portrait.”

“The portrait is one thing I still owe you,” said the farmer; “but the time will come when we'll manage what we can't manage now; and let me tell you, señor, if I could capture her grace and the height of her figure, it would amaze you; but that can't be done, because she's bent double, with her knees drawn up to her mouth; even so, anyone can see that if she could only stand upright, her head would knock against the ceiling; and she would already have given her hand in marriage to my bachelor, except that she can't stretch it out, being contracted as it is; yet even so, its long furrowed nails show how elegant and finely formed it is.”
“That will do, brother,” said Sancho; “consider her painted from head to foot. Now what is it you want? Come to the point without all this winding about, all these scraps and trimmings.”

“What I want, señor,” said the farmer, “is for your worship to do me the favor of a letter of recommendation to the girl's father, asking him to be so kind as to allow this marriage to go forward, since we are not badly matched, either in the gifts of fortune or in those of nature; for to tell you the truth, señor governor, my son is possessed by a devil, and not a day passes but the evil spirits torment him three or four times; and from having once fallen into the fire, his face is puckered up like a scrap of parchment, and his eyes are watery and forever running; but he has the temperament of an angel, and if he didn't thrash and pummel himself, he'd be a saint.”
“Is there anything more you want, good man?” asked Sancho.

“There is one more thing I'd ask,” said the farmer, “though I hardly dare mention it; but out it must come; after all, I can't let it sit rotting in my breast, whatever happens. What I mean, señor, is that I'd like your worship to give me three hundred or six hundred ducats toward my bachelor's marriage portion — to help him set up house; because they really must live on their own, free of the meddling of their fathers-in-law.”
“Think hard whether there's anything else you'd like,” said Sancho, “and don't be shy or modest about naming it.”
“No, truly, there is nothing,” said the farmer.

The instant he said it, the governor leaped to his feet, snatched up the chair he had been sitting in, and bellowed, “By all that's holy, you ill-mannered, clodhopping Don Bumpkin, if you don't clear out of here this second and get out of my sight, I'll split your head open with this chair. You whoreson scoundrel, you painter for the devil himself — at this hour you come asking me for six hundred ducats! Where would I get them, you stinking brute? And why would I give them to you if I had them, you knave, you blockhead? What do I care about Miguelturra or the whole tribe of the Perlerines? Out, I say, or by the life of my lord the duke I'll make good on my word. You're no man of Miguelturra — you're some rogue sent up from hell to tempt me. Why, you villain, I haven't held this government half a day, and already you want six hundred ducats out of me!”

The carver signaled the farmer to leave the room, which he did with his head hanging, looking for all the world terrified that the governor would make good on his threats — for the rogue knew very well how to play his part.

But let us leave Sancho to his fury, and peace be with the whole company; and let us return to Don Quixote, whom we left with his face bandaged and dressed after the cat wounds, which took eight full days to heal; and on one of those days there befell him something that Cide Hamete promises to recount with all the exactness and truthfulness he brings to every detail of this great history, however small it may be.
